name: Sterling-Nakamura PersonalAegis PA-7 'Rampart'
description:
A handheld hardlight projector that generates a 60-centimeter-diameter disc of semi-solid photonic matter, functioning as a personal shield capable of deflecting physical blows, absorbing low-velocity projectiles, and blocking chemical sprays. The PA-7 is the first consumer-grade hardlight product, adapted from Sterling-Nakamura's military hardlight barrier systems with drastically reduced power and duration to meet civilian safety standards and battery constraints.

The shield disc projects from a grip-activated emitter roughly the size of a flashlight handle. When activated, the disc materializes in approximately 0.3 seconds and maintains coherence for up to eight seconds per activation, with four activations per charge. The hardlight surface has the approximate stopping power of 6mm polycarbonate — sufficient to block a punch, a knife slash, or a low-velocity flechette round, but not rated against standard firearms ammunition or high-energy weapons.

Sterling-Nakamura prices the PA-7 at Φ2,400, firmly in the Tier 3-4 market segment. The device is marketed through personal security consultants and high-end lifestyle retailers, emphasizing its technological sophistication and the prestige of carrying hardlight technology. The limited eight-second activation window per use means the PA-7 is a reactive tool — something deployed in the critical seconds of an encounter rather than a sustained defensive system.
specifications:
shield diameter: 60 cm disc
activation time: 0.3 seconds
shield duration: 8 seconds per activation
activations per charge: 4
stopping power: equivalent to 6mm polycarbonate
weight: 320 g
length: 16 cm (handle)
recharge time: 4 hours
cost: Φ2,400
tactical_use: Deploy the shield between yourself and the immediate threat. The disc projects perpendicular to the handle axis, so hold the PA-7 like a flashlight pointed at the attacker. The eight-second window requires decisive action — deploy the shield, then immediately move to cover or escape. Against melee attackers, the hardlight disc can be used to physically push back — the surface is rigid enough to strike with. Not effective against firearms; do not rely on it to stop bullets.
cultural_context: The PA-7 is the first time hardlight technology has appeared in a consumer product, and Sterling-Nakamura has leveraged this heavily in marketing. Carrying a PA-7 is a statement that you have access to the cutting edge of materials science in your pocket. Tech enthusiasts and early adopters drove initial sales, but the device has found practical adoption among Tier 3-4 residents who transit through areas where knife crime and physical assault are common. The brief shield duration is a frequent criticism, but Sterling-Nakamura frames it as a design feature — the PA-7 gives you eight seconds, and eight seconds is enough to change an outcome.
story_hooks: A PA-7 was used to block a knife attack on a corporate executive, and the attacker's blade shattered against the hardlight surface — fragments injured bystanders, raising questions about whether defensive hardlight creates secondary hazards.

Sterling-Nakamura's military division is concerned that civilian PA-7 units are being reverse-engineered to understand hardlight emitter construction — consumer devices are appearing in black-market workshops where they are being studied for weaponization.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, compact handheld projector resembling a premium tactical flashlight crossed with medical instrumentation. The cylindrical body tapers slightly toward the emitter end, with an ergonomic grip that dominates the lower two-thirds. When activated, a brilliant disc of cyan-tinged hardlight materializes perpendicular to the axis—a semi-transparent barrier that shimmers with faint internal refraction patterns, like frozen aurora.
physical_description.dimensions: Handle: 16 cm length, 4.2 cm diameter. Active shield disc: 60 cm diameter when projected.
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively light in hand—320 grams feels almost insubstantial for something that generates solid light. The weight distribution is balanced toward the lower grip, making it feel wieldy even during rapid deployment.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade carbon composite body housing the photonic projection array, with embedded quantum capacitor cells visible through semi-translucent polymer sections along the barrel.
physical_description.finish: Satin brushed gunmetal with anodized aluminum accents. The emitter end is polished to mirror-bright finish, designed to focus the hardlight projection array.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: neutral gunmetal gray with brushed silver highlights. Accent: soft cyan LED charging indicators along the grip ridge. When active, the projected shield glows soft electric blue-white with spectral diffraction at the edges.
physical_description.grip_texture: Rubberized textured polymer with subtle diamond-pattern grip panels. Contoured for one-handed operation with an intuitive pressure-activation trigger integrated into the thumb rest.
distinctive_features: Transparent polycarbonate viewport running along the barrel—reveals the pulsing quantum capacitor cells within
Recessed grip-activation trigger with tactile feedback
Three small LED indicators (power status, charge level, overheat warning) clustered near the emitter
Precision-machined focus ring around the emitter for calibration
Subtle cooling vents as thin slots along the barrel to manage photonic projection heat
Engraved depth-of-field distance markers (in centimeters) etched below the grip
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Sterling-Nakamura logo embossed on upper grip in brushed chrome. Certification hologram (Tier 3+ licensed) inlaid into grip panel. Serial number laser-etched on the polished emitter rim. Small military-heritage insignia stamped near the base of the barrel—a nod to the PA-7's hardlight barrier ancestry.
physical_description.condition_typical: Factory-fresh units are pristine and mirror-polished. Field units show minor scuffing on the grip and faint heat-discoloration around the emitter from repeated photonic projection cycles. Well-maintained examples retain their mirror finish; heavy-use units develop fine scratches and a frosted patina on the barrel.
